articles.title: Washington Is About to Unlock Anthropic's Fable 5. India's Quiet Diplomacy Helped.
articles.excerpt: After two weeks of backdoor negotiations at the Pax Silica Summit, the US is close to restoring access to the AI model it abruptly shut down — and India's IT Secretary forced the conversation.
articles.image_caption: Server infrastructure in a modern data center — the physical backbone of the AI models at the centre of the US-India access dispute
articles.nri_angle: Indian developers and IT companies like TCS that were cut off from Claude Fable 5 on June 12 are about to regain access — but the episode has forced a reckoning over whether India can safely build its tech future on American AI platforms.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's VCs Just Poured $1.2 Billion into Deep Tech in Six Months. They're Not Funding Apps.
articles.excerpt: Drones, electric aircraft, gas turbines, and AI chips — India's venture capital scene is shifting from consumer apps to defence tech and hardware, and the money is moving fast.
articles.image_caption: Close-up of a microchip on a printed circuit board — the kind of hardware India's VCs are now willing to fund
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs in Silicon Valley, India's deep tech boom is creating the kind of technical challenge and equity upside that used to require staying in the Bay Area — defence drones, eVTOL aircraft, and sovereign AI chips are now fundable in Bengaluru.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Man Who Ran Infosys Just Raised $32 Million to Make It Obsolete
articles.excerpt: Vishal Sikka's new AI startup Hang Ten Systems wants to do what Indian IT giants do with thousands of engineers — but with agentic code generation and a fraction of the people.
articles.image_caption: Vishal Sikka, former Infosys CEO and founder of Hang Ten Systems
articles.nri_angle: Former Infosys CEO building AI-native IT services threatens the outsourcing model that employs millions of Indian engineers and sustains hundreds of thousands of H-1B jobs in the US.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Accenture's Growth Warning Just Wiped Billions Off Indian IT. The Real Threat Is Deeper.
articles.excerpt: A revenue guidance cut sent TCS and Infosys into freefall. But the bigger danger is an AI-native competitor class that could reshape who builds enterprise software — and who gets laid off first.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange, where the Nifty IT Index fell over 5% following Accenture's growth warning (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian IT stocks crashed after Accenture's guidance cut, threatening H-1B employment pipelines and NRI portfolios as AI-native vendors emerge to displace the traditional outsourcing model.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ambani's $180 Billion Jio IPO Is Finally Happening. NRIs Have a Seat Problem.
articles.excerpt: India's largest-ever listing is set for the second half of 2026. For Indian-Americans eager to invest, the real challenge is not the valuation — it's the paperwork.
articles.image_caption: Mukesh Ambani, chairman of Reliance Industries and the driving force behind the Jio Platforms IPO
articles.nri_angle: Jio's IPO is India's most-anticipated listing of the decade, and NRIs face practical investment hurdles including PIS account requirements, FEMA compliance, and FATCA reporting that may limit their participation.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Pichai's Google Just Told Meta to Get in Line. The AI Compute War Has a Waitlist.
articles.excerpt: Google has restricted Meta's access to Gemini AI models after Zuckerberg's team demanded more computing capacity than Alphabet could deliver. For Indian engineers at both companies, the rationing is reshaping daily work.
articles.image_caption: Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet and Google, in 2023
articles.nri_angle: Sundar Pichai's Google now controls AI infrastructure so essential that even Meta must queue for access — a power shift felt daily by tens of thousands of Indian engineers at both companies, and one driving the hyperscaler data centre race in India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The $11 Billion AI Lawyer Just Opened a Bengaluru Office. India Has 50 Million Reasons It Needs One.
articles.excerpt: Harvey AI, the world's most valued legal tech startup, is building products out of India, signing Flipkart and Reliance as clients, and hiring Indian-origin engineers to run its Bengaluru hub. India's clogged courts are the pitch.
articles.image_caption: International Tech Park in Bengaluru's Whitefield corridor, part of the city's tech ecosystem where Harvey AI has opened its India engineering hub (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs dealing with India's notoriously slow legal system — property disputes, inheritance claims, business litigation — stand to benefit as legal AI compresses the hours (and bills) lawyers spend on document review and case research.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Government Built Its Own GPT. It Speaks 22 Languages. The Talent to Scale It Lives Abroad.
articles.excerpt: BharatGen, the IIT Bombay-led AI consortium backed by a ₹1,058-crore government grant, has launched Param-2 — a 17-billion-parameter model covering all of India's scheduled languages. The problem is not funding. It is the deep tech talent deficit that only the diaspora can fill.
articles.image_caption: IIT Bombay campus — home to the BharatGen consortium leading India's sovereign AI mission
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin AI researchers dominate Silicon Valley labs but India's own sovereign AI push faces a severe talent deficit — BharatGen's success may depend on whether NRI talent can be channelled back through sabbaticals, advisory roles or returns.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A $100,000 Price Tag on Every H-1B Hire. A Judge Said No. The Government Said Wait.
articles.excerpt: The most controversial visa fee in US history is stuck in legal limbo, leaving tech companies and hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals planning for a cost nobody can confirm will stick.
articles.image_caption: A USCIS Application Support Center in New York, where H-1B visa petitions are processed
articles.nri_angle: Indian professionals hold 72% of H-1B visas, and the $100,000 fee directly impacts every tech worker's sponsorship economics — from startups deciding whether to hire internationally to IT services firms rethinking their US delivery models.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Amazon Just Dropped Another $13 Billion on India. The Hyperscaler Land Grab Is Getting Serious.
articles.excerpt: Andy Jassy's latest pledge lifts Amazon's total India commitment to $48 billion by 2030, making AWS the country's most aggressive cloud and AI infrastructure investor.
articles.image_caption: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, who announced the $13 billion investment after meeting PM Modi in New Delhi
articles.nri_angle: Amazon employs tens of thousands of Indians on H-1B visas globally. AWS India's infrastructure build-out creates high-paying engineering roles and makes returning to India more attractive for NRI cloud architects.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A War Far From Gujarat Is Threatening India's Chip Ambitions
articles.excerpt: Supply chain disruptions from the West Asia conflict are delaying specialty gases and metals critical to Tata Electronics' Dholera fab, raising fresh doubts about India's semiconductor timeline.
articles.image_caption: A researcher inspects a silicon wafer in a semiconductor fabrication cleanroom
articles.nri_angle: NRI semiconductor professionals considering a return to India's chip industry face new timeline uncertainty. Diaspora investors bullish on Tata Group's fab ambitions should factor in geopolitical supply risks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: OpenAI Poaches Uber India's President to Run Its Second-Largest Market
articles.excerpt: Prabhjeet Singh, who spent a decade scaling Uber across India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, becomes OpenAI's first managing director for the country as the AI race in the subcontinent intensifies.
articles.image_caption: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, whose company has hired Uber India president Prabhjeet Singh to lead its India operations (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: India is OpenAI's second-largest market; the appointment signals that Indian professionals aren't just building AI — they're running the business, with direct implications for NRI engineers, enterprise partners, and investors tracking the AI race.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm's Indian-Origin CFO Just Unveiled a $15 Billion Data Centre Bet. Meta and Microsoft Signed Up.
articles.excerpt: Akash Palkhiwala, an Ahmedabad-born engineer who has spent his entire career at Qualcomm, is steering the chipmaker's most ambitious pivot — from phone chips to AI infrastructure — with backing from two of tech's biggest spenders.
articles.image_caption: Qualcomm headquarters in San Diego, where the company unveiled its $15 billion data centre revenue roadmap
articles.nri_angle: Qualcomm's Indian-origin CFO Akash Palkhiwala is leading a $40 billion diversification bet; the pivot means new hiring in server and AI chip design — areas that overlap with India's engineering talent and Qualcomm's large Hyderabad and Bengaluru design centres.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nasscom Says AI Will Create a $400 Billion Market for Indian IT. Its Old Model Won't Get It There.
articles.excerpt: The industry body pitched AI as the next growth engine for India's outsourcing giants at a forum in the US. But the pivot from headcount billing to outcome-based delivery requires a workforce transformation that is barely under way.
articles.image_caption: An Infosys campus in Bangalore — India's 15 billion IT services industry is pivoting to artificial intelligence as Nasscom forecasts a 00 billion market opportunity (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs working at Indian IT firms on H-1B visas, the AI pivot means fewer task-execution roles but higher-value AI deployment and consulting positions — a workforce reshaping with direct implications for immigration and career planning.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sanjay Mehrotra's Micron Just Passed Meta in Market Value. His Secret Weapon: $22 Billion in Contracts Nobody Can Cancel.
articles.excerpt: The Indian-born CEO's take-or-pay revolution has made memory chips the hottest trade in AI — and his Gujarat fab the next frontier.
articles.image_caption: Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Micron Technology, at a 2025 industry event
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin CEO Sanjay Mehrotra (IIT, born Kanpur) runs America's only HBM chipmaker, now worth more than Meta; Micron's $2.75B Gujarat fab is India's biggest semiconductor investment.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Just Put a Padlock on GPT-5.6. Indian Developers Are on the Outside.
articles.excerpt: OpenAI's most powerful model launched to just 20 government-approved partners. For India's second-largest ChatGPT market, the wait has only begun.
articles.image_caption: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, at a meeting in February 2025
articles.nri_angle: India is OpenAI's second-largest market; millions of Indian developers and NRI-founded startups rely on ChatGPT API — the restricted GPT-5.6 launch means they trail American competitors by weeks.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Indian-Origin Founders Just Built a $2 Billion Chip Startup. Nvidia Invested Anyway.
articles.excerpt: Upscale AI's SkyHammer networking chip challenges Nvidia's own NVSwitch dominance — and the chip giant put money into the challenger. Premji Invest led the round.
articles.image_caption: Server racks inside a modern data centre — the kind of infrastructure Upscale AI's networking chips are designed to connect
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin serial entrepreneurs Barun Kar and Rajiv Khemani, backed by Premji Invest, are building foundational AI infrastructure — a signal of growing Indian founder dominance in deep-tech hardware, not just software.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hackers Just Published 630 GB of Apple's Manufacturing Secrets. They Got Them From Tata.
articles.excerpt: A ransomware group leaked 200,000 files from Tata Electronics — including TSMC documents marked 'Secret' and Qualcomm trade secrets. India's credibility as a manufacturing hub is on the line.
articles.image_caption: Bombay House, the global headquarters of the Tata Group in Mumbai (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: India now makes 26% of the world's iPhones. A massive data breach at its biggest Apple supplier tests the credibility of India's manufacturing ecosystem — and the NRI investment thesis behind it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Apple Is Quietly Shopping for a Second Chipmaker. Intel and Samsung Are Auditioning.
articles.excerpt: Preliminary talks with Intel and a Samsung factory visit signal Apple's first serious effort to break its TSMC dependency. The deal is years away — but Indian semiconductor engineers are already at the centre of it.
articles.image_caption: Apple CEO Tim Cook, who acknowledged chip supply constraints and is exploring alternative manufacturers
articles.nri_angle: Intel employs thousands of Indian-origin semiconductor engineers, and a foundry deal with Apple would expand hiring in a field where diaspora talent is concentrated. India's own Tata Dholera fab rides the same global capacity wave.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Biggest Insurtech IPO Lists on Monday. The Real Test Is Whether Anyone Buys Insurance Differently.
articles.excerpt: Turtlemint's ₹883 crore debut on BSE and NSE arrives into a market where 96 per cent of Indians still lack adequate health cover — and the company's bet is that half a million human advisors, armed with AI, can close that gap faster than any app alone.
articles.image_caption: The Bombay Stock Exchange, where Turtlemint begins trading on Monday in India's biggest insurtech IPO (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRI investors tracking India's insurtech sector get a rare public-market vehicle, while the platform's 'phygital' model mirrors how many diaspora families still buy insurance — through a trusted advisor, not an app.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian SaaS Company Just Bought a San Francisco AI Startup. The Direction of That Deal Says Everything.
articles.excerpt: MoEngage's acquisition of Aampe — and its simultaneous reverse merger to shift domicile back to India — signals that the country's enterprise software companies are done being the outsourced back office. They want to own the product.
articles.image_caption: Bengaluru's tech corridor — MoEngage, headquartered here and in San Francisco, is reversing the typical Indian startup playbook (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin SaaS founders who once flipped their companies to US holding structures are now re-domiciling to India — a reversal that has implications for NRI investors, employees, and the broader narrative of where enterprise value gets built.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Tech Job Market Hit a 28-Month Low. Thousands of Returning H-1B Workers Are Walking Into It.
articles.excerpt: Active tech openings fell to 93,000 in June. Senior roles collapsed 67 per cent. And 7,300 H-1B returnees in the first half of 2026 are discovering that the fallback plan no longer guarantees a soft landing.
articles.image_caption: Infosys campus in Electronic City, Bangalore — the heart of India's IT industry, now facing a 28-month low in tech job openings (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: The 'I'll go back to India' fallback plan no longer guarantees a soft landing. Indian engineers in the Bay Area and beyond face a tighter market at both ends — stricter US visa rules AND a domestic hiring collapse.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Meta Just Handed WhatsApp to a Mumbai Founder Who Never Wrote a Line of Code
articles.excerpt: Kunal Shah, the CRED founder who turned credit-card bills into a rewards empire, will lead the world's biggest messaging app. Meta is betting $900 million that an Indian entrepreneur can build the super-app Silicon Valley never could.
articles.image_caption: Kunal Shah, founder of CRED, now leads WhatsApp globally
articles.nri_angle: Shah joins Pichai, Nadella, and Mohan on the roster of Indian-origin leaders running global platforms — but as the first founder-CEO, not a corporate climber. NRI investors should watch CRED's IPO trajectory closely.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Indian-Origin CEO You've Never Heard Of Is Powering Every AI Data Centre on Earth
articles.excerpt: SiTime's Rajesh Vashist runs a precision timing chip company whose stock has doubled this year. His $3.2 billion Renesas deal and eight straight quarters of triple-digit growth make him the most important semiconductor CEO nobody is talking about.
articles.image_caption: Inside an AI data centre — SiTime's MEMS timing chips synchronize the components that power every major AI server cluster (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Vashist represents the Indian-origin deep-tech leadership layer that rarely makes headlines but is building the AI infrastructure stack. For NRI investors, SiTime offers a different template from IT services or consumer apps — hard-science semiconductor value.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's Central Bank Just Ordered a Kill Switch on Every AI System in Banking
articles.excerpt: The RBI's draft framework demands board-level oversight, mandatory human alternatives for customers, and the ability to shut down any AI model on command — the most prescriptive rules of their kind anywhere.
articles.image_caption: The Reserve Bank of India headquarters in Mumbai
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs hold Indian bank accounts, invest through AI-powered platforms, and send remittances via UPI — all systems now subject to the RBI's strictest-ever AI governance rules.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's First Private Orbital Rocket Is on the Launchpad. A Billion-Dollar Bet Rides on It.
articles.excerpt: Skyroot Aerospace, now valued at $1.1 billion with backing from Alphabet's Ram Shriram, GIC, and BlackRock, is weeks from attempting what no Indian private company has done.
articles.image_caption: Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-S rocket during its 2022 sub-orbital launch from Sriharikota
articles.nri_angle: Founded by IIT-trained ex-ISRO engineers and backed by Silicon Valley legend Ram Shriram, Skyroot's launch anchors a $44 billion space sector that NRI investors and professionals increasingly have stakes in.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nikesh Arora's Palo Alto Networks Hit an All-Time High. His Bet: AI Makes Hackers Worse, Not Cybersecurity Obsolete.
articles.excerpt: The Indian-born CEO used Anthropic's frontier model to find five years of vulnerabilities in six weeks. His $240 billion company has doubled while the market panicked over software's future.
articles.image_caption: Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, at TechCrunch Disrupt
articles.nri_angle: Indian-born Nikesh Arora, an IIT alum and former Google executive, leads the world's most valuable cybersecurity company at a moment when AI-driven threats are creating massive demand for security talent and platforms.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Big Tech's AI Glasses War Just Went Mass-Market. The Race for Your Face Has a Hindi-Speaking Contender.
articles.excerpt: Meta launched $299 smart glasses with its proprietary Muse Spark AI — which translates Hindi in real time. Google, Apple, and Snap are all scrambling to catch up. For NRIs, the stakes are quietly personal.
articles.image_caption: A person wearing augmented reality smart glasses — the form factor Big Tech is betting will define the AI era
articles.nri_angle: Meta's Muse Spark AI now translates Hindi in real time on its new glasses — the first mass-market wearable to bridge casual conversation between NRI parents visiting the US and their English-dominant grandchildren. Indian engineers at Meta, Google, and Qualcomm are building much of this hardware stack.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Apple Just Killed the M6 Pro and Max. The AI Chip It's Racing Toward Will Reshape What NRIs Pay for Macs.
articles.excerpt: Mark Gurman reports Apple will skip its high-end M6 chips entirely and jump straight to an AI-focused M7 lineup in 2027 — the first time Apple has ever scrapped a chip generation mid-cycle. Days after a painful price hike in India, the move raises more questions than it answers.
articles.image_caption: An Apple silicon processor — the chip family whose roadmap Apple just upended to prioritise AI
articles.nri_angle: Apple just raised prices across Macs and iPads in India by 5-10%, citing AI-driven memory shortages. Now it's killing the M6 Pro and Max chips — meaning NRI buyers and Indian developers who rely on MacBook Pro for professional work face a longer wait for the next meaningful upgrade, at higher prices.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: SK Hynix Dethroned Samsung After 25 Years. Now It Wants $29 Billion From Wall Street.
articles.excerpt: The memory chipmaker that nearly went bankrupt in 2002 is now South Korea's most valuable company, planning a Nasdaq ADR listing on July 10 that could be one of the largest in history.
articles.image_caption: High-bandwidth memory chips of the kind driving SK Hynix's rise to become South Korea's most valuable company (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRI investors get direct Nasdaq access to the AI memory boom on July 10; Micron's Gujarat fab feeds the same HBM supply chain; memory shortages are already raising Apple and Xbox prices for Indian-American consumers.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: ChatGPT Just Lost Its Majority. Pichai's Gemini and an Anthropic Revolt Are Why.
articles.excerpt: OpenAI's chatbot fell below 50% market share for the first time as Sundar Pichai's Gemini quietly reached 662 million users and Claude quadrupled on a wave of trust-driven migration.
articles.image_caption: Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet and Google, whose Gemini AI assistant has reached 662 million monthly users
articles.nri_angle: Sundar Pichai's Gemini is the biggest winner in the AI assistant race; Indian engineers in Silicon Valley are building multi-model stacks across ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude; India's download decline signals monetisation challenges ahead.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Five Eyes Says AI Cyberattacks Are Months Away. India's IT Sector Is Already Selling the Shield.
articles.excerpt: The intelligence alliance warned that frontier AI models will transform cyber warfare within months. For TCS, Infosys and a generation of Indian security professionals, the timing could not be better.
articles.image_caption: Hacker working at a computer terminal, illustrating the AI-accelerated cyber threat landscape
articles.nri_angle: Indian IT services firms like TCS, Infosys and Wipro are pivoting hard into cybersecurity as demand surges; India's domestic cyber market is growing at 20%+ annually; Indian-American security professionals face both a threat landscape and a career tailwind.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Apple Is Lobbying the White House to Buy Chips From a Blacklisted Chinese Firm. The Memory Crisis Left It No Choice.
articles.excerpt: Tim Cook's company approached the Commerce Department weeks ago, seeking clearance to buy from Chang Xin Memory Technologies. Days later, Apple raised iPad and MacBook prices and called the shortage a 'hundred-year flood.'
articles.image_caption: Apple Park in Cupertino, California — the company is lobbying the White House for an exemption to buy memory chips from blacklisted Chinese firm CXMT (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Apple price hikes hit Indian American consumers directly; Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra's Gujarat fab is the American answer to CXMT, and Apple sourcing from the Chinese rival would undercut it.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Jensen Huang Says Nvidia's China Revenue Has Dropped to Zero. The $20 Billion Vera CPU Is His Answer.
articles.excerpt: At his annual shareholder meeting, the Nvidia CEO declared the AI profitability era has arrived — and admitted China is lost. The Vera Rubin platform, designed for agentic AI, replaces that revenue entirely.
articles.image_caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a 2025 event
articles.nri_angle: Nvidia is one of Silicon Valley's largest H-1B employers of Indian engineers; India's data centre buildout — $48B from Amazon, $15B from Google — runs on Nvidia hardware, making this a direct diaspora infrastructure story.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's AI Startups Just Raised Over $1 Billion in Back-to-Back Rounds. The Bet Is Sovereignty.
articles.excerpt: Neysa, Sarvam, and Uniphore have collectively raised over $1 billion. After the U.S. restricted Anthropic's most advanced models, the case for Indian-built AI infrastructure is no longer theoretical.
articles.image_caption: Bengaluru, the hub of India's AI startup ecosystem, where companies like Krutrim and Sarvam AI are building sovereign AI infrastructure (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRI investors and engineers are watching India's AI ecosystem mature from services to infrastructure; the sovereign AI push triggered by Anthropic's Fable 5 restriction affects every Indian company running U.S.-built models.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Nadella Says a Few AI Labs Are Eating the World. He Just Signed a 20-Year Deal to Build His Own.
articles.excerpt: The Microsoft CEO published an essay, gave a pointed interview, launched a multi-model agent platform, and locked in 2.67 gigawatts of Texas power — all in two weeks. The strategy is clear: commoditise the model layer before it commoditises you.
articles.image_caption: Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin CEO of the world's most valuable tech company is reshaping the AI power structure — with direct implications for H-1B engineers and Indian IT professionals in Microsoft's orbit.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sundar Pichai Promised Gemini 3.5 Pro in June. Google Just Pushed It to July.
articles.excerpt: The delay comes as Flash 3.5 gains computer-use capability and Apple adds Gemini to Xcode — but OpenAI and Anthropic are not waiting.
articles.image_caption: Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet and Google
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin Alphabet CEO navigates a competitive AI race while thousands of Indian engineers at Google DeepMind build the models — and watch their RSU-heavy compensation move with every announcement.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The AI Trade Just Had Its Worst Week in Months. For Indian Tech Workers, the Pain Is Personal.
articles.excerpt: The Nasdaq lost 4.6 per cent, the Magnificent Seven shed $2.8 trillion in a month, and the stock-heavy pay packets that anchor diaspora life in Silicon Valley are shrinking fast.
articles.image_caption: jurvetson via flickr (BY)
articles.nri_angle: Indian tech workers at FAANG companies derive 40-60% of compensation from stock — a 15-25% monthly drawdown directly hits down payments, college savings, and stay-vs-return calculations, while H-1B holders face layoff vulnerability with only 60 days to find new sponsors.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Anthropic and AWS Just Launched an AI Accelerator in Bengaluru. The Bet Is That India Builds, Not Just Codes.
articles.excerpt: The India-first programme selects 40 startups building autonomous AI agents, marking another step in Bengaluru's quiet transformation from talent pool to AI product hub.
articles.image_caption: The International Tech Park in Bengaluru, the city Anthropic and AWS chose for their first joint AI startup accelerator (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: NRIs are watching India transition from an AI talent farm to an AI product hub — the accelerator alongside Sarvam's unicorn status and $48B in hyperscaler commitments is forcing the diaspora to reassess whether India is now a viable place to build, not just work remotely for US companies.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian-Origin Engineer Built Anthropic's Self-Improving AI. Now His Startup Is Worth $1 Billion.
articles.excerpt: Harsh Mehta's Mirendil raised $200 million from Nvidia, Andreessen Horowitz, and Kleiner Perkins to let any lab build AI that accelerates its own research — a capability the frontier giants keep to themselves.
articles.image_caption: A neural network visualization — Mirendil is building AI systems that can accelerate their own research, a frontier area of machine learning (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin CTO Harsh Mehta's trajectory from Google to Anthropic to a $1B startup illustrates how diaspora researchers at frontier AI labs are beginning to convert technical contributions into founding stakes and ownership, not just salaries.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Sundar Pichai's Alphabet Just Joined the Dow. It's Losing Nobel-Winning Researchers to Rivals.
articles.excerpt: Google's parent replaces Verizon in the 30-stock benchmark on June 29 — days after a Nobel laureate defected to Anthropic and a Gemini co-lead left for OpenAI, wiping $256 billion in a single session.
articles.image_caption: Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, whose company joins the Dow Jones Industrial Average on June 29
articles.nri_angle: Led by Indian-origin CEO Sundar Pichai, Alphabet's Dow inclusion is a milestone for diaspora tech leadership; NRI investors face both index-fund tailwinds and brain-drain headwinds.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Oracle Posted Record Profits and Then Fired 21,000 People. It Blamed AI.
articles.excerpt: The database giant disclosed the biggest AI-attributed workforce reduction in corporate history. Indian engineers on H-1B visas and fresh graduates with rescinded offers are among the hardest hit.
articles.image_caption: Oracle co-founder and CTO Larry Ellison, whose company disclosed 21,000 AI-driven job cuts
articles.nri_angle: Oracle is a major H-1B employer of Indian tech workers; layoffs trigger the 60-day visa clock, and rescinded campus offers in India freeze the entry pipeline for new graduates.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India's $315 Billion IT Industry Built Its Empire on Labour. AI Is Dissolving the Foundation.
articles.excerpt: TCS is cutting 12,000 jobs. Entry-level tech hiring has crashed 44 per cent. And the sector that employs six million people is facing a question it spent three decades avoiding.
articles.image_caption: The Wipro campus in Sarjapur, Bengaluru — one of many Indian IT campuses facing an AI-driven identity crisis
articles.nri_angle: NRIs hold heavy positions in Indian IT stocks, work for TCS/Infosys/Wipro US operations on H-1B/L-1 visas, and factor IT sector health into return-to-India decisions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Qualcomm Spent $4 Billion on Software That Speaks Every Chip's Language. The Target Is Nvidia's Walled Garden.
articles.excerpt: The $3.92 billion all-stock purchase of Modular is Cristiano Amon's clearest bet yet that Qualcomm's future is in data centres and AI software, not just the phone chips that built it.
articles.image_caption: Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon, who is steering the chipmaker's .92 billion acquisition of AI software startup Modular (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Indian engineers dominate Qualcomm's design centres in Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai, so a pivot from smartphone chips into data-center AI reshapes the work and the career ladder for tens of thousands of them.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: OpenAI Just Hired Uber's India Boss to Run the Country. The Job Is Less About Code Than Conquest.
articles.excerpt: Prabhjeet Singh, who spent a decade scaling Uber's India business, becomes OpenAI's most senior leader in a market it now treats as second only to the United States.
articles.image_caption: A smartphone running the ChatGPT app, the consumer product OpenAI is racing to scale in India
articles.nri_angle: For Indian engineers and founders, OpenAI building a real India org under a heavyweight operator signals jobs, India-specific pricing, and a faster pipeline of products that NRIs' families back home will actually use.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Amazon Just Promised India Another $13 Billion. The Real Story Is Who Gets to Own the Cloud Underneath the AI Boom.
articles.excerpt: Andy Jassy's pledge takes Amazon's planned India spend to $48 billion through 2030, deepening a hyperscaler land grab that runs straight through Mumbai and Hyderabad.
articles.image_caption: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, who announced the additional $13 billion India investment after meeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi
articles.nri_angle: Every NRI engineer working on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud has a stake in whether India becomes a core hyperscaler hub, because it determines where the next decade of cloud and AI jobs, data residency, and India-built products actually live.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Washington Just Got First Dibs on OpenAI's Newest Brain. The Indian Engineer Building on It Has to Wait in Line.
articles.excerpt: OpenAI is releasing GPT-5.6 to a short list of government-approved customers before the public, a precedent that lands hardest on the developers and startups outside the room.
articles.image_caption: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, whose company is staggering the release of GPT-5.6 at the U.S. government's request.
articles.nri_angle: The Indian-American developers, startup founders and cybersecurity engineers who build on top of OpenAI's models now face a future where access to the most powerful AI is rationed by Washington — a structural shift that reshapes who gets to compete.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Infosys Says AI Is a $400 Billion Prize, Not a Pink Slip. It's Still Hiring Freshers to Prove It.
articles.excerpt: While headlines tally six-figure IT job cuts, Salil Parekh is betting the opposite way — keeping campus hiring intact and pitching AI as the industry's largest revenue opening yet.
articles.image_caption: The glass pyramid at the Infosys campus in Mysuru, the company's flagship training center for new recruits.
articles.nri_angle: For NRI families whose children study engineering in India and aim for U.S. tech careers — and for the diaspora professionals invested in Infosys and TCS stock — whether the IT giants keep hiring freshers or quietly stop is the single clearest signal of where the pipeline to Silicon Valley still leads.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: An Indian Brand Wants to Sell You a ₹13,000 Phone Built on Its Own Software. The Pitch Is Privacy, Not Specs.
articles.excerpt: Madhav Sheth's Ai+ has launched the Nova 2 Pro and Neo, the latest push for an indigenous smartphone stack in a market still run by Chinese hardware and Google's Android.
articles.image_caption: A smartphone; the Indian brand Ai+ has launched the Nova 2 series running its own software stack, pitching privacy over specs in the sub-₹15,000 segment
articles.nri_angle: For NRIs who buy unlocked phones on India trips for relatives — and who track the 'Make in India' electronics story as both consumers and investors — an Indian-branded handset on a homegrown software layer is a test of whether the country can move up the value chain from assembly to design.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Man Who Ran Infosys Now Wants AI to Replace the Work That Built It
articles.excerpt: Vishal Sikka's new Palo Alto startup, Hang Ten, raised $32 million to deliver enterprise software with AI agents instead of armies of engineers — the exact model that employs hundreds of thousands of Indians.
articles.image_caption: Vishal Sikka, former Infosys CEO and founder of Hang Ten Systems, speaking at a SAP event.
articles.nri_angle: Hang Ten's AI-native delivery model directly threatens the IT-services jobs that built the Indian diaspora's H-1B pipeline — yet it is led by an Indian-origin ex-Infosys CEO and backed by Indian-American capital.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
